stem: An application wants the model to be able to call multiple independent tools in parallel within a single turn when appropriate (e.g. looking up weather for three cities at once), rather than being forced to call them one at a time across separate turns. What enables this?
explanation: The model can natively emit multiple `tool_use` blocks within a single turn when it determines several independent calls are appropriate; the client just needs to execute all of them and return all corresponding `tool_result` blocks together, rather than any special request flag being required to allow it.

choices.text: The model can emit multiple `tool_use` blocks in one turn on its own when appropriate; the client executes all of them and returns all corresponding `tool_result` blocks together.
choices.reasoning: Correct: parallel tool calling happens naturally within a single turn's content array when the model judges multiple independent calls are useful; the client's job is to fulfill all of them and report all results back.

choices.text: Parallel tool calls require submitting the request through the Batches API instead of a real-time call.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: parallel tool calls within one turn are a real-time Messages API behavior and have nothing to do with the separate asynchronous Batches API.

choices.text: Parallel tool calls are impossible; the model can only ever request one tool call per turn.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: a single turn's content array can contain multiple `tool_use` blocks, enabling multiple calls to be requested together.

choices.text: Parallel tool calls require setting temperature to 0.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: temperature controls sampling randomness and has no bearing on whether the model chooses to request multiple tool calls in one turn.

stem: A model version an application depends on is announced for deprecation with a future retirement date. What is the recommended course of action?
explanation: Applications should plan and test a migration to a supported model version ahead of the retirement date, since continuing to call a retired model identifier after that date will start failing; waiting until the deadline passes risks an unplanned outage.

choices.text: Plan and test a migration to a currently supported model version well ahead of the retirement date.
choices.reasoning: Correct: proactively migrating and validating behavior against a supported model before the deprecated one is retired avoids a sudden production failure on the retirement date.

choices.text: Ignore the deprecation notice since old model versions continue to work indefinitely regardless of announced retirement dates.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: deprecated model identifiers do eventually stop working after their retirement date; ignoring the notice risks an outage.

choices.text: Immediately switch to a random other model without testing, since all models behave identically.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: different models can have materially different behavior, so a migration should be tested and validated, not chosen at random.

choices.text: Contact Anthropic to request the old model never be retired.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the appropriate response to a deprecation notice is to migrate within the timeline provided, not to attempt to prevent the retirement from happening.

stem: Beyond the API's built-in prompt caching, an application also implements its own response cache keyed on the exact user query, storing full responses to avoid calling the API again for repeated identical questions. How does this differ conceptually from prompt caching?
explanation: Application-level response caching stores and reuses entire completed answers for identical requests, avoiding the API call altogether, whereas prompt caching (an API feature) still calls the model but reduces the cost/latency of reprocessing a shared prefix; they address different parts of the problem and can be used together.

choices.text: Application-level response caching skips calling the model entirely for repeated identical requests, whereas prompt caching still calls the model but cheaply reuses a processed prefix.
choices.reasoning: Correct: these are complementary but distinct techniques: one avoids the API call altogether for exact repeats, the other reduces cost within a call that still happens by reusing already-processed prompt content.

choices.text: They are exactly the same mechanism implemented at two different layers with no meaningful difference.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: they operate differently and address different situations (avoiding the call entirely vs. reducing cost/latency of a call that still happens), so they aren't functionally identical.

choices.text: Application-level caching is only possible if prompt caching is disabled.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: there is no such mutual exclusivity; an application can use both an application-level response cache and API-level prompt caching together.

choices.text: Prompt caching eliminates the need for the model to ever be called again for any future request.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: prompt caching still involves calling the model on every request; it just makes reprocessing a shared prefix cheaper, unlike application-level caching which can skip the call entirely.

stem: How does an application typically enable the citations feature for a document provided as a content block?
explanation: Citations are typically enabled per document via a citations configuration on that document's content block, opting that specific source into passage-level attribution rather than being a global, always-on request setting.

choices.text: By setting a citations configuration (e.g. enabling it) on the specific document content block being provided as a source.
choices.reasoning: Correct: citations are opted into per source document via that block's configuration, letting an application choose which sources should support passage-level attribution.

choices.text: Citations are always on for every request with no way to configure them.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: citations are an explicit, configurable feature tied to specific document content blocks, not an always-on default.

choices.text: By passing a separate citations API key distinct from the main API key.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: there is no separate citations-specific API key; citations are configured within the normal request using the same credentials.

choices.text: By setting temperature to exactly 0.5.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: temperature is a sampling parameter unrelated to whether citation attribution is enabled for source documents.

stem: If an error occurs partway through an otherwise-successful stream (after some content has already been sent), how is this typically communicated to the client?
explanation: A mid-stream error is communicated via a dedicated `error` event type within the SSE stream, letting the client detect that generation was interrupted abnormally rather than completing normally, distinct from the standard `message_stop` termination.

choices.text: Via a dedicated error event within the stream, distinct from the normal `message_stop` completion event.
choices.reasoning: Correct: streaming defines an explicit error event type so clients can detect an abnormal interruption instead of confusing it with a normal, successful stream completion.

choices.text: The connection simply closes with no indication of what happened.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: an explicit error event is emitted specifically so the client isn't left to guess why the stream ended abnormally.

choices.text: The client must poll a separate status endpoint to learn that an error occurred mid-stream.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the error is communicated inline within the same stream via an error event, not through a separate polling mechanism.

choices.text: Mid-stream errors are impossible once generation has started.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: errors can still occur after generation has begun (e.g. transient server issues), which is exactly why a dedicated error event exists in the streaming protocol.

stem: A request includes an image whose `media_type` field says `image/png` but the actual bytes are a JPEG file. What is the likely outcome?
explanation: A mismatched or incorrect `media_type` can cause the image to be misinterpreted or rejected, since the API relies on the declared `media_type` to correctly decode the provided bytes; the `media_type` must accurately describe the actual image data.

choices.text: The image may be misinterpreted or rejected, since the API relies on the declared `media_type` matching the actual encoded image data to decode it correctly.
choices.reasoning: Correct: the `media_type` field is not just a label; the API uses it to decode the bytes correctly, so a mismatch between declared and actual format can cause decoding failures or errors.

choices.text: The API automatically detects the true format and ignores the declared `media_type` entirely, with no issue.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the declared `media_type` is used to interpret the bytes, so relying on the API to silently `fix` a mismatch is not a safe assumption.

choices.text: This has no effect; `media_type` is purely informational metadata that is discarded.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: `media_type` is functionally used for decoding, not merely decorative metadata that gets ignored.

choices.text: The request will always succeed and produce identical results regardless of the mismatch.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: a mismatch between declared and actual image format is a real integration bug that can cause errors or incorrect processing, not something guaranteed to be harmless.

stem: A developer wants to explicitly prevent the model from calling any tools for a specific request, even though tools are defined in the request (perhaps for consistency with other calls), forcing a plain text-only answer. Which `tool_choice` setting accomplishes this?
explanation: `tool_choice` {'type': 'none'} explicitly disables tool calling for that request, forcing a text-only response even if a tools array is present, which is useful for maintaining one consistent request-building code path while still controlling behavior per call.

choices.text: `tool_choice: {"type": "none"}`
choices.reasoning: Correct: this setting explicitly forces a text-only response, preventing any tool call even when tools are defined in the request.

choices.text: `tool_choice: {"type": "auto"}`
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: `auto` still allows the model to choose to call a tool if it judges that appropriate; it does not force a text-only answer.

choices.text: Omitting the tools array entirely is the only way to prevent tool calls.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: `tool_choice` `none` allows tools to remain defined in the request while still preventing their use, without needing to remove the tools array.

choices.text: `tool_choice: {"type": "any"}`
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: `any` forces the model to call some tool, the opposite of preventing tool use.

stem: For a streamed response containing a `tool_use` block, how should the client reconstruct the full `input` JSON for that tool call?
explanation: The `tool_use` block's input arrives as a series of `partial_json` string fragments across multiple `input_json_delta` events; the client must concatenate these fragments in order and parse the resulting complete string as JSON once the block closes.

choices.text: Concatenate the `partial_json` fragments from successive `input_json_delta` events in order, then parse the fully assembled string as JSON once the block ends.
choices.reasoning: Correct: tool input streams as incremental string fragments that only form valid JSON once fully concatenated, so the client must accumulate them before attempting to parse.

choices.text: Each `input_json_delta` event already contains complete, independently parseable JSON.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: individual fragments are typically partial and not independently valid JSON; only the fully concatenated string is guaranteed to parse correctly.

choices.text: The full tool input is always delivered in a single `content_block_start` event with no deltas needed.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: tool input streams incrementally via deltas after `content_block_start`, rather than arriving whole in the start event.

choices.text: Tool input cannot be reconstructed from a stream; a second non-streaming request is required to get it.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the full tool input is fully recoverable by correctly accumulating the streamed deltas; no second request is necessary.

stem: An internal tool used only by trusted employees on a company VPN still routes its Claude API calls through a backend rather than calling the API directly from a desktop client app. What is a reasonable justification for this, beyond key protection?
explanation: Even for trusted internal use, routing through a backend centralizes concerns like usage monitoring/auditing, consistent prompt/version management, and the ability to change providers or add safeguards without redistributing client software, in addition to the baseline benefit of not distributing the secret key.

choices.text: Centralizing calls through a backend also enables consistent usage monitoring, centralized prompt/version management, and the ability to change behavior without redistributing client software.
choices.reasoning: Correct: beyond hiding the key, a backend proxy gives operational control (auditing, centralized configuration, easy updates) that would otherwise require redistributing and updating every desktop client individually.

choices.text: There is no reasonable justification; internal trusted tools should always call the API directly from the client.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: a backend proxy offers real operational advantages even for trusted internal usage, so this isn't accurate.

choices.text: A backend is required because desktop applications are technically incapable of making HTTPS requests.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: desktop apps can make HTTPS requests directly; the reasons for a backend proxy are architectural/operational, not a technical limitation of desktop networking.

choices.text: It is required because the API only accepts requests from server-classified IP ranges.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: there is no such IP-classification requirement on the API; the justification here is about operational control, not a technical API restriction.

stem: A team building a customer-facing chatbot wants to show a friendly fallback message instead of a raw stack trace whenever any API call fails. Where should this fallback logic live?
explanation: Fallback handling belongs in the application's own error-handling layer wrapping API calls (catching the SDK's typed exceptions or checking HTTP error responses), translating technical failures into a user-appropriate message, rather than expecting the API itself to return pre-formatted UI text.

choices.text: In the application's own error-handling layer around each API call, catching failures and translating them into an appropriate user-facing message.
choices.reasoning: Correct: the API returns structured technical error information; it is the application's responsibility to catch that and present something appropriate to the end user.

choices.text: The API automatically returns a pre-formatted, friendly UI message whenever any error occurs.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the API returns structured technical error details (status codes, error types), not ready-made UI copy; translating that into a friendly message is the application's job.

choices.text: This can only be done by disabling streaming for all requests.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: whether streaming is enabled has no bearing on where user-facing fallback error handling should be implemented.

choices.text: Fallback messaging isn't possible; users must always see the raw error object.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: nothing prevents the application from catching an error and displaying custom, user-friendly messaging instead of raw error details.

stem: A batch request that individually would have failed with a context-length error is included among thousands of otherwise-valid requests in one batch submission. How is this reflected in the final batch results?
explanation: That specific request's result entry reports its own error (mirroring what a standalone real-time call would have returned), while the rest of the batch's requests are processed and reported independently and unaffected by that one failure.

choices.text: That specific request's result entry reports its own error, matching what a standalone call would have returned, without affecting the other requests in the batch.
choices.reasoning: Correct: batch processing evaluates each request independently, so an individual failure is captured in that request's own result entry, leaving the rest of the batch's outcomes unaffected.

choices.text: The entire batch is marked as failed and no results are returned for any request.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: a single request's failure does not cascade to invalidate the entire batch; other requests still complete and report their own results normally.

choices.text: The failing request is automatically retried with a shorter prompt by the API.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the API does not automatically rewrite or shorten a failing request's content on the client's behalf; the failure is simply reported as-is.

choices.text: The failing request is silently dropped from the results file with no trace.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: failed requests still appear in the results with their error information, rather than being silently omitted.

stem: When an SDK call exhausts its configured `max_retries` without success, what does the SDK typically do?
explanation: Once retries are exhausted, the SDK raises an exception (representing the final failure) back to the calling code, which is then responsible for its own handling, such as logging or surfacing a fallback response.

choices.text: It raises an exception representing the final failure, which the application code then handles.
choices.reasoning: Correct: after exhausting configured retries, the SDK surfaces the failure as an exception rather than silently succeeding or hanging indefinitely, leaving handling to the caller.

choices.text: It silently returns an empty successful response as if nothing went wrong.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: a silent fake-success response would hide real failures from the application; SDKs surface the failure explicitly instead.

choices.text: It automatically switches to a different, unrelated API provider.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: SDKs are scoped to the Claude API and do not fail over to a different provider on their own.

choices.text: It retries indefinitely forever, ignoring the configured `max_retries` value.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: `max_retries` is exactly the configured ceiling on retry attempts; exceeding it stops further automatic retries and surfaces the failure.

stem: An application exposes a runtime feature flag that toggles between two different models for a given feature, to compare quality and cost in production. What must the team be careful to keep consistent when comparing results across the flag?
explanation: When comparing model variants, other request parameters (prompt content, temperature, `max_tokens`, tool definitions, etc.) should be held constant across the flag so any observed difference in quality, cost, or latency can be attributed specifically to the model change rather than confounded by other varying settings.

choices.text: Keep all other request parameters (prompt, temperature, `max_tokens`, tools, etc.) constant across both flag variants.
choices.reasoning: Correct: for a valid comparison, only the variable under test (the model) should differ; letting other parameters vary too would confound the results and make conclusions unreliable.

choices.text: Nothing needs to be held constant; any two configurations can be validly compared regardless of other differences.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: allowing multiple parameters to differ simultaneously makes it impossible to attribute observed differences specifically to the model change.

choices.text: Only the API key needs to differ between the two variants.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the API key is unrelated to which model is used or to the validity of a model comparison; it doesn't need to differ at all for this test.

choices.text: The system prompt must be different for each model to get a fair comparison.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: deliberately varying the system prompt alongside the model would introduce a second variable, undermining a controlled, fair comparison.

stem: An application needs to extract structured data (e.g. line items and totals) from photographed receipts at scale. Which combination of features fits this well?
explanation: Combining vision input (to read the receipt image) with a tool-based structured output pattern (a tool schema describing the desired fields) lets the application reliably get validated structured data extracted from unstructured image input.

choices.reasoning: Incorrect: images are sent as image content blocks, not converted into system prompt text; the system parameter carries text instructions, not image bytes.

stem: How is the depth of a model's extended thinking typically controlled by the developer?
explanation: Extended thinking is configured with a thinking budget (a token allowance dedicated to internal reasoning before the final answer), which the developer sets based on how much deliberation the task warrants, trading off latency/cost against reasoning depth.

choices.text: By setting a thinking token budget that allocates how many tokens the model may use for internal reasoning before producing its final answer.
choices.reasoning: Correct: the thinking budget is the configurable lever controlling how much reasoning effort (and associated latency/cost) the model is allowed to spend before answering.

choices.text: By adjusting the `top_p` parameter, which directly controls reasoning depth.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: `top_p` affects nucleus sampling of the output distribution, not the amount of internal reasoning the model performs.

choices.text: Extended thinking depth cannot be configured; it is always fixed regardless of the task.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the thinking budget is an explicit, developer-configurable setting, not a fixed, unconfigurable behavior.

choices.text: By changing the `stop_sequences` list.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: `stop_sequences` define strings that halt generation; they have no relationship to how much internal reasoning budget the model is given.

stem: Which use case is a poor fit for the Message Batches API?
explanation: An interactive chat feature where the user is actively waiting in real time for a response is a poor fit for batch processing, since batches are designed for asynchronous, non-latency-sensitive workloads rather than immediate, conversational turnaround.

choices.text: A live customer-facing chat interface where the user is actively waiting for an immediate reply.
choices.reasoning: Correct: batches trade immediacy for cost efficiency, making them unsuitable for interactive scenarios where a user is waiting in real time for a response.

choices.text: Nightly bulk classification of a large archive of support tickets where results are reviewed the next morning.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this is a strong fit for batch processing, since it is large-volume, asynchronous, and not latency-sensitive.

choices.text: Generating summaries for tens of thousands of documents as part of an offline data pipeline.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this is exactly the kind of large-scale, non-interactive workload batch processing is designed for.

choices.text: Re-processing a large historical dataset once a quarter for a report.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this is a good batch use case, being large-volume, infrequent, and non-time-critical.

stem: A client's retry logic retries on every non-2xx response uniformly, including 400 errors caused by a bug that sends slightly malformed JSON for one specific request type. What operational problem does this cause?
explanation: Retrying a deterministic client-side bug (like malformed request construction) will simply keep failing identically on every attempt, wasting retry budget and delaying failure visibility, rather than fixing anything, since the underlying request never changes between attempts.

choices.text: The retries will keep failing identically since the underlying malformed request never changes between attempts, wasting time/requests and delaying detection of the actual bug.
choices.reasoning: Correct: retrying a deterministic request-content bug produces the same failure every time; it doesn't recover anything and just masks/delays discovering the real problem in request construction.

choices.text: This causes no operational problem since retries always eventually succeed no matter the cause of failure.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: a deterministic bug in request construction will fail identically on every retry; there's no reason it would eventually succeed just from repeated attempts.

choices.text: The API will automatically fix the malformed JSON on the client's behalf after enough retries.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the API validates and rejects malformed requests; it does not attempt to repair or guess at the client's intended, correctly-formed request.

choices.text: It has no downside because 400 errors are always transient just like 429 errors.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: 400 errors reflect a problem with the request content itself and are not transient in the way 429/5xx errors are; treating them identically is the actual problem being described.

stem: Can prompt caching be applied to a large, frequently reused reference PDF sent as a document content block?
explanation: `cache_control` can be applied to a document content block just like other content types, so a large reference PDF that is reused across many requests can be cached to avoid the cost of reprocessing it on every call.

choices.reasoning: Correct: caching is not limited to text/system content; document content blocks can be marked with `cache_control` the same way, which is valuable for large, repeatedly referenced documents.

choices.text: No; caching only applies to plain text content, never to documents or images.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: caching applies to content blocks generally, including document and image content, not exclusively plain text.

choices.text: No; PDFs must be re-uploaded and reprocessed fully on every single request with no way to avoid this.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: both the Files API (avoiding re-upload) and prompt caching (avoiding reprocessing cost) directly address this concern for reused documents.

choices.text: Yes, but only if the PDF is fewer than two pages long.

stem: A developer testing a streaming integration notices the final accumulated text differs slightly from what a non-streaming call with identical parameters returns on a different attempt. What is the most likely explanation?
explanation: Absent temperature 0 and other determinism-affecting settings, sampling-based generation can vary between separate calls regardless of whether streaming is used; streaming versus non-streaming is a delivery mechanism and does not itself change what content is generated for a given call.

choices.text: Natural sampling variability between separate generation calls, not a difference caused by streaming versus non-streaming delivery itself.
choices.reasoning: Correct: streaming only changes how the same underlying generation is delivered to the client; any variation between separate calls stems from normal sampling behavior, not from the streaming mechanism itself.

choices.text: Streaming responses are inherently lower quality than non-streaming responses.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: streaming does not alter generation quality; it only changes delivery mechanics.

choices.text: Streaming truncates the response at a fixed shorter length than non-streaming calls.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: `max_tokens` governs length identically regardless of streaming; streaming does not impose a separate, shorter truncation point.

choices.text: Non-streaming responses always ignore the system prompt.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the system prompt is applied identically whether or not the response is streamed.
